summary: Describes the policy for registering second-level domains under the .MIL domain. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The rules for who can get a web name ending in .mil, which is reserved for the military.

questions: how to register a mil domain
subtitle: Rules for military organizations to register under the .mil domain.

tldr.problem: The .MIL domain needed clear rules for which organizations could register domain names and how they would be managed.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC establishes that only US military services and DoD commands can register directly under .mil; other DoD organizations register under their service's domains. The DoD NIC manages all registrations and requires at least two DNS servers.
tldr.outcome: The policy ensures the .mil namespace remains controlled and properly configured for military Internet operations.

facts.label: Eligible organizations
facts.value: US military services and DoD commands

today: RFC 1956 is an Informational RFC from June 1996 that remains in effect as the governing policy for .MIL domain registration.

sections.title: Military Domain Policy
sections.content: RFC 1956 describes the policy for registering second-level domains under the .MIL domain, which is delegated from the Internet root authority to the US Department of Defense. This RFC ensures proper governance of a critical namespace used exclusively for military Internet operations.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC explains the rules for the .mil domain, which is used only by the US military.

sections.title: Who Can Register
sections.content:
Only US military services, unified or specified commands, and DoD operating agencies that do not report through military service chains can register directly as second-level domains under .MIL. All other DoD organizations must register through their respective military service's second-level domain, not directly under .MIL.

The DoD Network Information Center (DoD NIC) administers the entire .MIL domain and processes all registration requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the main military branches and top DoD commands can have their own .mil domains. Other military offices must use their branch's domain.

sections.title: Registration Requirements
sections.content:
Domain names under .MIL must be descriptive and preferably 12 characters or less. Names are unique on a first-come-first-served basis. Each domain must be supported by at least two name servers located in separate networks. Critically, all DNS servers supporting .MIL subdomains must themselves be located in the .MIL domain.

Applicants must submit a registration template to the DoD NIC hostmaster at hostmaster@nic.ddn.mil, and only registered .MIL users are accepted as domain administrators.
sections.plainLanguage: Every .mil domain needs at least two backup name servers, and domain names should describe what organization they serve.
